Cyclic TES Discharge Mode. One case each for heating and cooling mode (Test #5) corresponded to unit-on/off cycling, where the TES discharges for 15 minutes, followed by 15 minutes with the unit off. This operating mode mimics an on/off cycling pattern for a thermostatically controlled heat pump. It is thus one of the most critical tests of system performance for real-world integration. Continuous TES Charge Mode at Extreme Ambient Temperatures. One case each for heating and cooling mode (Test #10) corresponded to continuous unit operation in TES charging mode at extreme ambient temperatures, i.e., heating mode charging at cold- climate heat pump conditions when winter-peaking utilities may most require demand reduction (H4 , DBT = 5°F/-15°C) and cooling mode charging at a high ambient Full temperature (DBT = 105°F/40.6°C) that may occur during times of day when excess solar power generation results in low-cost electricity. In both cases, the TES heat losses are expected to significantly impact the time and energy required to fully recharge the TES units. Cyclic TES Charge Mode with Intermittent Base HP Mode Space Conditioning. One case each for heating and cooling modes (Test #4) corresponded to a cyclic operation in which the TES is charged for 15 minutes, followed by 15 minutes of base HP space conditioning. This operating mode could occur when a thermostat calls for space conditioning occurs during off-peak hours when TES charging is scheduled. As human comfort is the primary objective of any heat pump system, such a test is critical to demonstrate that the HP-TES can switch between passive TES charging and active space conditioning. Intermittent TES Charge / Discharge Mode. The final test case (Test #11) corresponded to a cyclic unit operation in which the unit was cycled between 15 minutes of TES charging and 15 minutes of TES discharging for at least 2 hours, or until the TES was completely discharged. Such a test allows for exploring the benefits of TES heat transfer from repeated transient operation and may inform future control architectures to improve overall HP-TES system performance.
